authentication: none (anonymous calls work); optional free API key only raises the daily quota
cost_notes: free; no SLA and no commercial support; FDA may throttle or restrict access per its terms
entity_identifiers: PMA number (pma_number) + supplement_number - together they identify the record
UNKNOWN - no UDI-DI on the PMA record
free_tier: free; no key needed (1,000 req/day per IP); free key raises it to 120,000/day
historical_coverage: PMA originals and supplements; 57,421 records in the 2026-11-02 bulk export
known_limitations: a supplement is a separate record under the same pma_number; counting rows instead of distinct pma_number inflates the number of approved devices
same date problem as 510(k): decision_date is an event date, not a publication date
high-risk Class III only - it is not a substitute for the 510(k) stream and covers a much narrower slice of the five firms' portfolios
company linkage inherits the same submitter-string fragmentation as 510(k)
licence: public domain: FDA dedicates openFDA content/data to the public domain under a Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal dedication (open.fda.gov/license/, verified)
rate_limits: documented: 240 requests/min and 1,000 requests/day per IP without a key; 240/min and 120,000/day with a free key (open.fda.gov/apis/authentication/, verified). `skip` is capped at 25,000, so full history requires splitting by decision_date windows
research_value: PMAs mark the highest-risk device approvals, so they are the cleanest signal for frontier-technology launches (structural heart, neurostimulation, insulin pumps) where Medtronic and Philips compete. Supplement records additionally reveal post-approval label expansions, which 510(k) clearances do not expose as cleanly.
